facts.statement: The genus Dakosaurus was established by Friedrich August von Quenstedt in 1856.
facts.quote: authority: von Quenstedt, 1856

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Geosaurus maximus.
facts.quote: type_species: Geosaurus maximus

facts.statement: Two species are currently recognized: Dakosaurus maximus and Dakosaurus andiniensis.
facts.quote: subdivision: * Dakosaurus maximus (Plieninger, 1846) Dakosaurus andiniensis Vignaud & Gasparini, 1996

facts.statement: Dakosaurus is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph belonging to the family Metriorhynchidae.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph within the family Metriorhynchidae

facts.statement: Dakosaurus had large, serrated teeth that were flattened from side to side.
facts.quote: It was large, with teeth that were serrated and compressed lateromedially (flattened from side to side)

facts.statement: Dakosaurus was a carnivore that likely spent most or all of its life in the ocean.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus was a carnivore that spent much, if not all, of its life out at sea

facts.statement: The genus was named in 1856 based on a tooth originally described as Geosaurus maximus in 1846.
facts.quote: The genus was established by Friedrich August von Quenstedt in 1856 for an isolated tooth named Geosaurus maximus by Theodor Plieninger in 1846

facts.statement: The type species D. maximus is known from Late Jurassic fossils found in England, France, Switzerland, and Germany.
facts.quote: The type species Dakosaurus maximus, meaning "greatest biter lizard", is known from fossil discoveries in Western Europe (England, France, Switzerland and Germany) of the Late Jurassic (Late Kimmeridgian-Early Tithonian)

facts.statement: Early isolated teeth of Dakosaurus were initially mistaken for belonging to the dinosaur Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: When isolated Dakosaurus teeth were first discovered in Germany, they were mistaken for belonging to the theropod dinosaur Megalosaurus

facts.statement: Von Quenstedt created the new genus Dakosaurus in 1856 for the teeth previously named Geosaurus maximus.
facts.quote: In 1856 von Quenstedt made Plieninger's Geosaurus maximus teeth a new genus with the name Dakosaurus

facts.statement: Von Quenstedt named the genus Dakosaurus after the Greek word for 'bite' because of its terrible set of teeth.
facts.quote: He explained the etymology as Greek dakos "Biss" [bite] in 1858 in German, adding "denn wenige kommen seinem furchtbaren Gebiss gleich" [for few can match its terrible set of teeth]

facts.statement: Remains once attributed to Megalosaurus schnaitheimi are now considered to belong to Dakosaurus maximus.
facts.quote: Named in 1871 by Emanuel Bunzel, the remains attributed to Megalosaurus schnaitheimi (found in Schnaitheim, Germany) are now believed to have belonged to Dakosaurus maximus as per Carrano et al. (2012)

facts.statement: Fossils of Dakosaurus have been found in Late Jurassic deposits across England, France, Switzerland, Germany, Poland, Russia, Argentina, and Mexico.
facts.quote: Fossil specimens referrable to Dakosaurus are known from Late Jurassic deposits from England, France, Switzerland, Germany, Poland, Russia, Argentina, and Mexico

facts.statement: The species D. andiniensis was first reported in 1985 from the Neuquén Basin in Argentina.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus andiniensis, meaning "biter lizard from the Andes", was first reported in 1985 from the Neuquén Basin, a very rich fossil bed in the Vaca Muerta, Argentina

facts.statement: The formal name Dakosaurus andiniensis was established in 1996.
facts.quote: However, it was not until 1996 that the binomen Dakosaurus andiniensis was erected

facts.statement: D. andiniensis has a unique short, tall snout that earned it the nickname 'Godzilla' in press reports.
facts.quote: Two later discovered skulls, the specimina MOZ 6146P and MOZ 6140P, have indicated that D. andiniensis is unique among the metriorhynchids (the family of stem-crocodilians most specialised for marine life) with its short, tall snout, which lent it the popular nickname "Godzilla" in press reports about its description

facts.statement: D. andiniensis lived from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: This species has a fossil range from the late Jurassic to early Cretaceous (Late Tithonian-Early Berriasian)

facts.statement: All known species of Dakosaurus were large, reaching about 4 to 5 meters in length with skulls and jaws up to 1 meter long.
facts.quote: Description All currently known species would have been large, measuring approximately 4 - 5 m long, with skull and jaws approaching 1 m in length

facts.statement: Dakosaurus had a streamlined body and a tail with a large fin, making it a more efficient swimmer than modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Its body was streamlined for greater hydrodynamic efficiency, which along with its downturned tail supporting a large fin (known from soft-tissue impression on relatives) made it a more efficient swimmer than modern crocodilian species

facts.statement: While limbs were reduced, the femur remained robust, measuring 32 cm in one specimen and 43 cm in the neotype.
facts.quote: As with other metriorhynchids, the forelimbs were extremely reduced, the hindlimbs underwent a similar process, but the femur was still relatively large and robust, with that of a complete specimen described in 2026 being 32cm, and the one on the neotype measuring 43cm in length

facts.statement: The skull was triangular with large openings that housed strong muscles for a powerful bite.
facts.quote: In dorsal view, it is triangular in shape, with a much wider posterior portion, showcasing large supratemporal fenestrae which would've housed strong jaw adductor musculature for a stronger bite-force

facts.statement: Dakosaurus had large, few teeth compared to its relatives.
facts.quote: Teeth The teeth of Dakosaurus are characteristic in being large and few in number, compared to its relatives

facts.statement: The teeth interlocked like those of gharials and killer whales when the jaws were closed.
facts.quote: As evidenced by occlussion notches on the jaws and articulated skulls, the teeth interlocked in a fashion analogous to gharials and killer whales when the mouth was closed

facts.statement: Wear on the teeth suggests they ground against each other to shear flesh, indicating a macrocarnivorous diet.
facts.quote: Wear facets also indicate the teeth contacted against, and grinded each other down, likely a flesh-shearing adaptation for a macroredatory diet

facts.statement: Specimens from the Argentinian species preserve the chamber for well-developed salt glands, similar to other metriorhynchids.
facts.quote: Salt glands The incomplete skull specimens from the Argentinian species of Dakosaurus preserves the chamber in which the well-developed salt glands (known from Geosaurus and Metriorhynchus) would have been housed, and similarly enlarged peorbital fossae are present in other specimens

facts.statement: A 2012 study reclassified D. manselii into the genus Plesiosuchus to resolve issues with the paraphyletic nature of Dakosaurus.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus–when it contained the species D. andiniensis, D. maximus, and D. manselii–had long been considered paraphyletic, that is, not consisting of a common ancestor and its descendants, until a 2012 study moved D. manselii to the formerly invalid genus Plesiosuchus

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that niche partitioning allowed multiple crocodyliform species to coexist.
facts.quote: Alongside three other metriorhynchid species, it has been hypothesised that niche partitioning enabled several species of crocodyliforms to co-exist

facts.statement: Dakosaurus and Geosaurus giganteus were likely top predators in the Solnhofen limestone ecosystem.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus and Geosaurus giganteus would have been top predators of this Formation, both of which were large, short-snouted species with serrated teeth

facts.statement: A 2026 study reported cartilaginous fish remains found within the abdominal region of a new D. maximus specimen.
facts.quote: A 2026 study which redescribed the phylogenetic affinites of Dakosaurus also described a new specimen of D. maximus from the Kimmeridgian Torleite Formation of Germany, and report evidence of preservation of cartilaginous fish (likely hybodontiform) remains within the specimen's abdominal region

facts.statement: Dakosaurus fossils range from the Oxfordian to the Berriasian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Oxfordiense - Berriasiense (Jurásico Superior - Cretácico Inferior)

facts.statement: Dakosaurus belongs to the family Metriorhynchidae.
facts.quote: familia: Metriorhynchidae

facts.statement: Dakosaurus is classified within the subfamily Geosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Geosaurinae

facts.quote: synonyms: * Dacosaurus Sauvage, 1873} Megalosaurus schnaitheimi Bunzel, 1871

facts.statement: Dakosaurus was a large animal with serrated edges and laterally compressed teeth.
facts.quote: Era un animal grande, con dientes aserrados en los bordes y comprimidos en ambos lados.

facts.statement: The genus was established by Friedrich August von Quenstedt in 1856 based on an isolated tooth previously named Geosaurus maximus by Plieninger.
facts.quote: El género fue establecido por Friedrich August von Quenstedt en 1856 para un diente aislado llamado Geosaurus maximus por Plieninger.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus was a carnivore that spent most, if not all, of its life in the sea.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus era un carnívoro que pasaba la mayor parte de su vida, si no toda, en el mar.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dakosaurus gave birth in the water like dolphins and ichthyosaurs or laid eggs on the coast like turtles, as no eggs or nests are known.
facts.quote: la cuestión de si paría como los delfines y los ictiosaurios o anidaba en las costas como las tortugas es un misterio.

facts.statement: Isolated Dakosaurus teeth first found in Germany were initially misidentified as belonging to the theropod dinosaur Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Cuando se descubrieron por primera vez en Alemania dientes aislados de Dakosaurus, se interpretaron erróneamente como pertenecientes al dinosaurio terópodo Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Fossil specimens of Dakosaurus are known from Late Jurassic deposits in England, France, Switzerland, Germany, Poland, Russia, Argentina, and Mexico.
facts.quote: Especímenes fósiles referibles a Dakosaurus son conocidos de yacimientos del Jurásico tardío de Inglaterra, Francia, Suiza, Alemania, Polonia, Rusia, Argentina, y México.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus andiniensis lived from the end of the Jurassic to the early Cretaceous (Late Tithonian to Early Berriasian).
facts.quote: Esta especie tiene un rango temporal desde el fin del Jurásico hasta principios del Cretácico (Titoniense tardío - Berriasiense inicial).

facts.statement: Dakosaurus had a hydrodynamic body and a finned tail, making it a more efficient swimmer than modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Su cuerpo era hidrodinámico para mayor eficiencia en su desplazamiento por el agua, lo que junto a su cola con aleta lo hacía un nadador mucho más eficiente que los actuales cocodrilos.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus and Geosaurus giganteus were likely the top predators in the Solnhofen formation, both possessing large short-snouted skulls and serrated teeth.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus y Geosaurus giganteus era probablemente los depredadores superiores en esta formación, teniendo ambos grandes cráneos de hocico corto y dientes aserrados.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus was the only marine crocodiliform to evolve both laterally compressed and serrated teeth, which were larger than those of any other metriorhynchid.
facts.quote: Dakosaurus fue el único crocodiliforme marino que evolucionó dientes tanto comprimidos lateralmente como aserrados; no sólo eso, sino que eran mucho más grandes que los de cualquier otro tipo de metriorrínquido.

facts.statement: Large abductor muscles anchored in the supratemporal fenestrae of Dakosaurus skulls ensured a powerful bite.
facts.quote: Las fenestras supratemporales de los cráneos de Dakosaurus deben haber tenido anclados grandes músculos abductores (que se encargan del cierre de las mandíbulas), asegurando así una poderosa mordida.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus was likely capable of feeding by twisting to tear chunks of meat from its prey.
facts.quote: los dakosaurios deben haber sido capaces de alimentarse girando (desgarrando pedazos de carne de sus presas potenciales).

facts.statement: The parent group of Dakosaurus is Dakosaurina.
facts.quote: Parent group: Dakosaurina

facts.statement: Dakosaurus is classified in the class Reptilia.

facts.statement: Dakosaurus lived from the Callovian to the Aptian, between 165.3 and 113.2 million years ago.
